acquisition.why: Inbound is possible through Product Hunt, SEO and content, but DesignJoy's launch success depended on the founder's story and his network. Getting attention in a crowded category needs ongoing founder-led content [E].

onboarding.why: Clients subscribe and pay on the website with no calls. An agent can collect the brief with a form plus LLM triage.

delivery.why: Design work that clients find acceptable still needs a skilled human eye. AI helps with drafts, but brand and UX quality and revision loops need review on every request. Ricardo is technical, not a designer.

billing.why: Stripe subscriptions with pause and cancel run unattended.

support.why: Unlimited-request models create constant back-and-forth, revision disputes and scope arguments.

scores.R_why: An 'unlimited design' offer cannot be served on 6-8 h/week. The founder reached hospitalisation-level workload on a full-time basis. Ricardo would need to subcontract designers, which eats the margin and the £300 budget. A narrow, capped productized offer, such as AI-assisted landing pages for SaaS limited companies, is more plausible [E].
scores.M_why: Hundreds of DesignJoy clones exist, and AI design tools (Canva AI, Figma AI, v0, Lovable) commoditise the low end. Buyers increasingly do it themselves.
scores.one_line: The claims are real and widely reported, but it is a founder-labour business in a saturated, AI-eroded niche. Agents can run billing and intake, not the design quality that is the actual product.

acquisition.why: Etsy, Gumroad, Notion/Framer template galleries and SEO give inbound demand without outreach. This is platform-dependent, and the source notes Fiverr has dropped digital products.

onboarding.why: Buyers check out on the marketplace or store with no interaction.

billing.why: Handled by the marketplace or Stripe/Lemon Squeezy, including UK/EU VAT via a merchant of record.

support.why: Occasional 'how do I use this' and refund requests. Agents can answer most from docs.

scores.R_why: Cheap to test within £300. Ricardo can build technical templates (Notion, Airtable, spreadsheets, code starters) in short sessions. No regulatory issues beyond consumer terms and a merchant-of-record setup for VAT.
scores.M_why: Template marketplaces are flooded, and LLMs can generate many templates on request. Winners need a niche plus distribution. Revenue per seller is typically small [E].
scores.one_line: Highly automatable and cheap, but the evidence is vague (no claims) and the market is crowded and AI-commoditised. Only a sharp technical niche gives a small, mostly passive income.

acquisition.why: Paid social and SEO for a 'test your AI IQ' quiz can run through agents. Quizzes spread well. Ad spend scales with budget and needs human approval.

onboarding.why: Email-gated quiz with automated scoring. The opt-in form provides PECR consent.

delivery.why: Self-serve test and courses run unattended once built. Content needs periodic refresh as AI tools change.

billing.why: Stripe one-off checkout. The source shows a misconfiguration once killed all sales, so it needs testing.

support.why: Refund requests and questions about certificate value. Agents can handle most.

scores.R_why: Buildable by Ricardo cheaply. However, an unaccredited 'certification' needs careful wording under UK consumer protection law (CMA guidance on misleading claims). £300 of ads gives only a thin test [E].
scores.M_why: Free AI courses and certificates from Google, Microsoft, LinkedIn and Anthropic undercut paid $19-59 products. An unknown certification has little perceived value. B2B employee assessment is the more defensible angle [E].
scores.one_line: The automated funnel shape is attractive, but the only evidence is about 150 signups and zero sales. An unknown AI certificate competes with free big-brand credentials.

acquisition.why: The demand side (stalkers searching) can be reached via SEO and content. The supply side needs drone operators to list. Many are sole traders, so cold DMs or emails to them are restricted by PECR. Recruitment must come through inbound content, forums or ads [E].

onboarding.why: Self-serve listing form. An agent can verify CAA operator ID.

delivery.why: A directory with postcode search runs unattended.

support.why: Listing edits, disputes about lead quality and stale listings. Mostly agent-handled.

scores.R_why: Thermal-drone deer recovery exists in the UK, but the market is far smaller than in the US. UK deer stalking is a niche with few operators, and CAA rules (Open/Specific category, night flying) limit supply. Ricardo has no audience in shooting or stalking [E]. Applying the directory model to another UK drone niche, such as roof surveys, might suit better.
scores.M_why: There is little UK competition in this exact niche, but total addressable revenue is probably tiny: tens of pilots at a few hundred pounds a year [E]. Broader drone directories already exist.
scores.one_line: Directory mechanics are near-perfect for agents, and the US claims are first-hand and specific. The UK deer-recovery niche looks too small to matter, and the model would need a better UK vertical.

acquisition.why: Cluely grew through viral controversial content. Google and Meta ad policies may reject 'cheat in interviews' ads, so the business relies on organic virality.

delivery.why: Software with LLM API calls. It needs to keep ahead of detection by interview platforms.

support.why: Technical issues during live interviews are time-critical, and refund demands are likely.

scores.R_why: Ethically problematic: it facilitates deceiving employers and may expose Ricardo to complaints, platform bans and reputational harm in his own industry. Real-time low-latency audio and screen tooling is non-trivial to build on 6-8 h/week.
scores.M_why: Crowded with funded players (Cluely, Final Round AI, Interview Coder and others). Employers are moving to in-person and proctored interviews and detection tools.
scores.one_line: Evidence is second-hand VC valuations, not revenue. The space is crowded, ethically dubious and under active countermeasures, so it is not a fit.

acquisition.why: The source relies on outreach to local businesses, many of which are sole traders and so off-limits for cold email or DMs under PECR. Cold email to limited companies and inbound SEO are possible but highly competitive.

onboarding.why: Brand and voice intake plus social account access can be form-driven. It still needs client calls in practice.

delivery.why: AI drafts and schedules posts. Client approval and edits on each batch need human oversight.

support.why: Requests for changes, engagement complaints and churn conversations need human attention.

scores.R_why: Retainer clients expect responsiveness, and Ricardo has little time and no sales or marketing background. Low ticket sizes (£200-500/month [E]) and high churn.
scores.M_why: Extremely saturated. Meta AI, Canva and Buffer increasingly let owners do it themselves.
scores.one_line: Six videos discuss it, but the only first-hand claim is about staffing savings, not the model. Outreach-dependent, saturated and AI-commoditised, so a poor agent-run UK fit.

acquisition.why: UK self-storage is found inbound via Google Maps, SEO, Stashbee-type marketplaces and roadside visibility.

onboarding.why: Online booking, e-signature and smart-lock or code access can be automated.

delivery.why: Physical: buying containers, delivery, site security, damp and maintenance.

billing.why: Automated recurring billing. Arrears and lien processes need human action.

support.why: Access problems, theft, damp claims and site issues need someone on site.

scores.R_why: Containers cost about £2-4k each [E] plus land. Land near Bromley is expensive or Green Belt, and UK planning (change of use), business rates and insurance apply. This is far beyond a £300 test and 6-8 h/week.
scores.M_why: UK self-storage demand is solid and container storage is established, but local competition and planning are barriers.
scores.one_line: A viable real-world business, but evidence is all second-hand US anecdote. It is capital-heavy, physical and blocked by planning permission, so it is not agent-run or £300-testable.

acquisition.why: Content, SEO, YouTube and LinkedIn posting can be agent-drafted. Building an audience still needs a consistent personal voice.

onboarding.why: An email opt-in form with clear consent is PECR-compliant and fully automated.

billing.why: Affiliate payouts and back-end product sales are automated, but this is a funnel, not a revenue source in itself.

scores.R_why: Cheap and suited to Ricardo's skills (vibe-coded tools as lead magnets). It only pays if paired with a monetisable niche and back end, and it requires audience building over months.
scores.M_why: Gated PDFs and tools are everywhere, and AI makes them trivial, so attention is the scarce resource. Affiliate revenue is volatile.
scores.one_line: A highly automatable tactic, not a standalone business. Worth using as the acquisition layer for another product, with modest, first-hand-supported evidence.
